scenes.head: Discounting cash flows
scenes.sub: Most real streams of money are uneven: a loan pays interest and then its principal, a project costs money now and returns different amounts later. Learn to value any stream by discounting each cash flow, to judge a decision by its net present value, and to find the rate of return that makes that value zero.

segs.say: Discounting cash flows. Most real streams of money are uneven: a loan pays interest and then its principal, a project costs money now and returns different amounts later. Learn to value any stream by discounting each cash flow, to judge a decision by its net present value, and to find the rate of return that makes that value zero.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Construct a timeline for an uneven stream of cash flows and calculate its present value, or its value at any other date, by discounting each flow.
Calculate the net present value of a decision and use it to accept or reject the decision, explaining what a positive NPV means.
Price a fixed-rate note at the current market rate and explain why its value moves in the opposite direction to interest rates.
Estimate an internal rate of return by trial and interpolation, and explain how it relates to NPV and where it can mislead.
Use spreadsheet NPV and IRR functions correctly, including the timing of the first cash flow.

scenes.head: On 1 March 2026 Lantern borrowed $10,000 from Coastline Bank on a two-year note at 6% a year: $150 of interest every quarter and the $10,000 repaid…

segs.say: On 1 March 2026 Lantern borrowed $10,000 from Coastline Bank on a two-year note at 6% a year: $150 of interest every quarter and the $10,000 repaid on 1 March 2028. It is now 1 March 2027 and the quarterly payment due today has just been made. Four payments remain: $150 on 1 June, 1 September and 1 December 2027, and $150 plus the $10,000 principal on 1 March 2028. A similar loan now costs 8% a year compounded quarterly (fictional, like Coastline itself). Ana wants to know what the note is worth today, both to Coastline, which could sell the loan to another lender, and to Lantern, which owes it. The previous lesson valued the principal alone at $9,238.45. Now the interest comes in too.

chapters.title: A stream is a set of single amounts

scenes.head: A cash-flow stream is a series of amounts due at different dates.

segs.say: A cash-flow stream is a series of amounts due at different dates. When the amounts are equal and evenly spaced, the stream is an annuity, and module 3 gives formulas that value it in one step. Most real streams are uneven: a project’s cash flows rise and fall, a contract pays different sums at different dates, and a note like Lantern’s pays small amounts of interest and then one large sum. The method for any stream is the one you already have, applied once per amount. Put each cash flow on the timeline, discount it to time 0 with its own discount factor, and add the present values. Adding is now allowed, because every value is at the same date.
PV = C₁/(1 + r) + C₂/(1 + r)² + … + Cₙ/(1 + r)ⁿ = Σₜ₌₁ⁿ Cₜ/(1 + r)ᵗ

scenes.head: Here Cₜ is the cash flow at the end of period t and r is the rate per period.

segs.say: Here Cₜ is the cash flow at the end of period t and r is the rate per period. For the note, the periods are quarters and the rate is 8% ÷ 4 = 2% a quarter. The table discounts each payment.
Lantern’s Coastline note on 1 March 2027, discounted at 2% a quarter

Each of the note’s four remaining payments is discounted to 1 March 2027 with its own factor; the present values are then added. Almost all of the value comes from the final payment of interest and principal.

scenes.head: In March 2027 the note is worth $9,809.61 at the market rate.

segs.say: In March 2027 the note is worth $9,809.61 at the market rate. It promises $10,600 in all, $600 of interest and the $10,000 principal, but those dollars arrive over the coming year, and the market now pays 8% for waiting while the note pays only 6%. That shortfall makes the note worth $190.39 less than its $10,000 face value.

scenes.head: The two sides see the same number.

segs.say: The two sides see the same number. If Coastline sold the loan, a buyer who can earn 8% compounded quarterly elsewhere would pay no more than about $9,810 for it, so Coastline would take a loss of about $190. Lantern sees the mirror image: its obligation is worth $9,809.61 at today’s rates, and the $190.39 is what it gains, in today’s money, from having borrowed at 6% in 2026 instead of at 8% now. That is a good reason to keep the note to maturity rather than replace it with a new loan.

scenes.head: When rates rise, fixed payments are worth less

segs.say: When rates rise, fixed payments are worth less. A note, loan or bond with fixed payments falls in value when market rates rise and rises when they fall. At exactly its own rate, 6% compounded quarterly, Lantern’s note is worth exactly $10,000: discounting the interest at the rate it is paid gives back the principal. Above 6% the note is worth less than its face value; below 6%, more.

chapters.title: From value to decision: net present value

scenes.head: A stream’s present value says what it is worth.

segs.say: A stream’s present value says what it is worth. A decision usually has money going out as well as coming in, typically a cost now and benefits later. The net present value (NPV) of a decision is the present value of all its cash flows, with money received counted as positive and money paid as negative, discounted at the discount rate: the return you could earn elsewhere on an investment of similar risk.
NPV = C₀ + C₁/(1 + r) + C₂/(1 + r)² + … + Cₙ/(1 + r)ⁿ = Σₜ₌₀ⁿ Cₜ/(1 + r)ᵗ

scenes.head: C₀ is the cash flow today, usually a cost and so negative.

segs.say: C₀ is the cash flow today, usually a cost and so negative. It is not discounted, because it is already at time 0. A positive NPV means the decision returns more than the next-best use of the money, by that many dollars in today’s money: it adds value. A negative NPV means the money would do better elsewhere. The rule follows: accept a decision with a positive NPV and reject one with a negative NPV.

scenes.head: Lantern faces exactly this question this month.

segs.say: Lantern faces exactly this question this month. A cold-brew brewing system for the cafés and catering costs $24,000 (the canned Cold Brew planned for later in the year would be made by a co-packer, as M02 and M04 assume). Ana estimates the extra cash it would bring in, after paying for the beans, milk, bottles and staff time: $6,000 in the first year, $8,500 in the second and $9,000 in each of the third and fourth years, when she expects to sell the brewer for about $2,500. These estimates are fictional, and uncertain. For a risky small-business project she asks a return of 12% a year, the figure she judges she could earn elsewhere at similar risk. Worked example 3 discounts the estimates: the NPV is about +$1,848, so on her numbers the brewer is worth buying. How to pay for it, with Coastline’s 48-month loan or the supplier’s instalment plan, is a separate financing question, which the lessons on annuities and loan amortisation answer.

chapters.title: The rate that makes NPV zero

scenes.head: NPV depends on the discount rate.

segs.say: NPV depends on the discount rate. The higher the rate, the less the later inflows are worth and the lower the NPV, so somewhere it crosses zero. The rate at which it does is the decision’s internal rate of return (IRR): the rate of return the investment itself earns, period by period. For the brewer it is about 15.3% a year. Because 15.3% is above the 12% Ana requires, the IRR gives the same verdict as the NPV.

scenes.head: There is no general formula for the IRR, because the rate sits inside several powers at once.

segs.say: There is no general formula for the IRR, because the rate sits inside several powers at once. The classic method is trial and error. For a conventional project, a cost followed by inflows, try a rate and compute the NPV; if it is positive, try a higher rate, if negative a lower one, and close in on zero. Spreadsheets and financial calculators do the same thing, only faster. This lesson introduces the idea; F05 Corporate Finance uses NPV and IRR to make investment decisions in depth.

chapters.title: The value of a stream at any date

scenes.head: A stream can be valued at any comparison date T, not only today: each cash flow is moved to T, compounded if it comes earlier and discounted if it…

segs.say: A stream can be valued at any comparison date T, not only today: each cash flow is moved to T, compounded if it comes earlier and discounted if it comes later, and the results are added: V_T = Σₜ Cₜ (1 + r)^(T − t). Values at different dates are linked by a single factor: V_T = PV × (1 + r)^T. That gives a useful check.

scenes.head: Valued at 1 March 2028 (quarter 4), the note’s payments are worth 150 × 1.02³ + 150 × 1.02² + 150 × 1.02 + 10,150 = 10,618.24 dollars: what a holder…

segs.say: Valued at 1 March 2028 (quarter 4), the note’s payments are worth 150 × 1.02³ + 150 × 1.02² + 150 × 1.02 + 10,150 = 10,618.24 dollars: what a holder would have if she reinvested each interest payment at 2% a quarter until the note matured. And 9,809.61 × 1.02⁴ = 10,618.24, the same. Choosing the date where the question lives, today for a price and the end for a savings balance, saves work; it never changes the answer.

chapters.title: Matching the rate to the timing

scenes.head: The formulas assume each cash flow arrives at the end of a period, that time 0 is today, and that the rate is the rate per period of the same length…

segs.say: The formulas assume each cash flow arrives at the end of a period, that time 0 is today, and that the rate is the rate per period of the same length as the spacing. With quarterly cash flows you need a quarterly rate. If the rate you are given is quoted differently, convert it first, as the lesson on effective annual rates shows: an APR compounded quarterly is divided by 4; an effective annual rate becomes a quarterly rate of (1 + EAR)^(1/4) − 1.

scenes.head: When cash flows fall at irregular dates, measure each date in years from today, tᵢ, and discount with the effective annual rate: PV = Σᵢ Cᵢ ÷ (1 +…

segs.say: When cash flows fall at irregular dates, measure each date in years from today, tᵢ, and discount with the effective annual rate: PV = Σᵢ Cᵢ ÷ (1 + EAR)^(tᵢ). Worked example 2 does this for payments due in 0, 9, 12 and 24 months. Annual cash flows in a business plan are a simplification: the brewer’s sales arrive week by week, not in one lump at each year end. Treating them as year-end amounts slightly understates their value, and analysts accept that in exchange for a simpler model, or switch to monthly periods when the difference matters.

chapters.title: Signs and whose point of view

scenes.head: Every cash flow is someone’s inflow and someone else’s outflow.

segs.say: Every cash flow is someone’s inflow and someone else’s outflow. From Coastline’s side the note’s payments are inflows worth +$9,809.61; from Lantern’s side the same payments are outflows worth −$9,809.61. Pick one point of view for a whole problem and keep it. Financial calculators and spreadsheets use the same convention, money received positive and money paid negative, which is why a cost today must be entered with a minus sign.

chapters.title: Net present value in more depth

scenes.head: Three choices decide whether an NPV means anything.

segs.say: Three choices decide whether an NPV means anything.

The rate. The discount rate is the return the money could earn in its next-best use at similar risk: its opportunity cost. A riskier stream is discounted at a higher rate. For a business this is linked to its cost of capital, but a project riskier than the business as a whole deserves a higher rate. The rate on a loan used to pay for the project is not, by itself, the right rate: the loan rate prices the lender’s fairly safe claim, while the project’s cash flows are less certain.

The cash flows. Only incremental cash flows count: cash that changes because of the decision. Money already spent and unrecoverable is a sunk cost and is left out. NPV uses cash, not accounting profit: depreciation, for example, is not a cash flow.
The horizon. Every cash flow the decision causes belongs in the stream, including those at the end, such as the brewer’s resale value or the cost of removing equipment.

scenes.head: NPVs add up.

segs.say: NPVs add up. The NPV of two independent projects together is the sum of their NPVs, and the NPV of a project financed at a fair market rate is not changed by the financing. A financing offer that comes only with the purchase and costs less than the market rate, such as a supplier’s cheap instalment plan, has a value of its own that adds to the project’s NPV; it never changes the rate used to discount the project’s cash flows. When options exclude each other, such as two different brewers for the same counter, choose the one with the highest NPV, provided it is positive. Plotting NPV against the discount rate gives an NPV profile. For a conventional project, one cost followed by inflows, the profile slopes down and crosses zero once, at the IRR.

scenes.head: Estimates are uncertain, so an NPV should be recalculated under other assumptions.

segs.say: Estimates are uncertain, so an NPV should be recalculated under other assumptions. If every year’s cash from the brewer were 10% lower than Ana expects, its NPV at 12% would fall from +$1,847.77 to −$578.13. Without the $2,500 resale value it would be only +$258.98. A positive NPV that disappears under a small change in the estimates is a close call, not a clear win.

chapters.title: Internal rate of return: definition and trial

scenes.head: The IRR is the rate that solves 0 = Σₜ₌₀ⁿ Cₜ ÷ (1 + IRR)ᵗ.

segs.say: The IRR is the rate that solves 0 = Σₜ₌₀ⁿ Cₜ ÷ (1 + IRR)ᵗ. Take a two-year investment of $1,000 that returns $600 at the end of each year. At 10% its NPV is −1,000 + 600 ÷ 1.1 + 600 ÷ 1.21 = 41.32; at 15% it is −24.57. The IRR lies between them. A straight line between the two points crosses zero at

scenes.head: With only two periods the equation is a quadratic and can be solved exactly: the IRR is 13.07%.

segs.say: With only two periods the equation is a quadratic and can be solved exactly: the IRR is 13.07%. Linear interpolation overshoots slightly, because the NPV profile curves (it is convex), so the straight line lies above it. Checking the NPV at 13.14% gives −$0.96, slightly negative, and a second interpolation closes the gap. With more periods there is no neat formula, and calculators and spreadsheets repeat this kind of step until the NPV is close enough to zero.

scenes.head: For a conventional project, an IRR above the required return and a positive NPV are the same statement, so the two rules agree.

segs.say: For a conventional project, an IRR above the required return and a positive NPV are the same statement, so the two rules agree. The IRR has limits. When cash flows change sign more than once, for example a project with a large clean-up cost at the end, the equation can have more than one IRR, or none. When choosing between options of different sizes or timing, the one with the higher IRR can have the lower NPV: over one year, when money costs 10%, a 50% return on $1,000 adds less value than a 20% return on $100,000. In those cases trust the NPV. F05 Corporate Finance treats these issues fully.

scenes.head: For a loan or a bond bought at a given price and held to maturity, the IRR has another name: its yield to maturity.

segs.say: For a loan or a bond bought at a given price and held to maturity, the IRR has another name: its yield to maturity. A buyer who paid $9,809.61 for Lantern’s note on 1 March 2027 and received the four payments would earn exactly 2% a quarter, 8% a year compounded quarterly, because that is the rate used to price it. A buyer who paid $10,000 would earn the note’s own 6%.

chapters.title: Spreadsheets: NPV, IRR and the first cash flow

scenes.head: Spreadsheet functions save time but carry a trap.

segs.say: Spreadsheet functions save time but carry a trap. Excel’s NPV(rate, value1, value2, …) treats the first value as arriving one period from now, at the end of period 1. A cash flow at time 0 must be left out of the range and added separately: =C0 + NPV(r, C1:Cn). Microsoft’s own documentation says the first value must be added to the NPV result rather than included in the values. Put the time-0 cost inside the range and every cash flow is discounted one period too many, so the result is the true NPV divided by 1 + r: for the brewer, $1,649.80 instead of $1,847.77.

scenes.head: IRR(values), by contrast, expects the whole stream including the time-0 flow, and returns the rate per period.

segs.say: IRR(values), by contrast, expects the whole stream including the time-0 flow, and returns the rate per period. IRR() needs at least one negative and one positive value, and it searches from a starting guess (10% unless you give one), so when the cash flows change sign more than once it reports only one of the possible rates. For cash flows at irregular dates, XNPV and XIRR take a list of dates as well as amounts. Whatever the tool, lay out the timeline first, so you know which cash flow sits at which date before you type a formula.

scenes.head: Present value of an uneven stream

segs.say: Present value of an uneven stream: PV = Σₜ₌₁ⁿ Cₜ/(1 + r)ᵗ.
PV: Present value of the stream at time 0 ($).
Cₜ: Cash flow at the end of period t (positive if received, negative if paid) ($).
r: Discount rate per period, as a decimal (per period).
t: Period in which the cash flow arrives (periods).
n: Last period with a cash flow (periods).
It assumes this: Cash flows at the end of each period; one rate per period throughout.
When all the C_t are equal, the annuity formulas of module 3 give the same answer in one step.

scenes.head: Value of a stream at any date

segs.say: Value of a stream at any date: V_T = Σₜ Cₜ (1 + r)^(T − t) = PV × (1 + r)^T.
V_T: Value of the whole stream at period T ($).
Cₜ: Cash flow at period t ($).
r: Rate per period, as a decimal (per period).
T: The comparison date (periods).
t: Period in which the cash flow arrives (periods).
PV: Value of the stream at time 0 ($).
Flows before T are compounded forward; flows after T are discounted back.

scenes.head: Net present value

segs.say: Net present value: NPV = Σₜ₌₀ⁿ Cₜ/(1 + r)ᵗ = C₀ + C₁/(1 + r) + … + Cₙ/(1 + r)ⁿ.
NPV: Net present value of the decision ($).
C₀: Cash flow today, usually a cost (negative) ($).
Cₜ: Incremental cash flow at the end of period t ($).
r: Discount rate per period: the return available elsewhere at similar risk (per period).
t: Period in which the cash flow arrives (periods).
n: Last period with a cash flow (periods).
It assumes this: Only incremental cash flows; sunk costs left out; the rate reflects the risk of the cash flows.
Accept if NPV > 0; among options that exclude each other, choose the highest NPV, provided it is positive.

scenes.head: Present value with irregular dates

segs.say: Present value with irregular dates: PV = Σᵢ Cᵢ/((1 + EAR)^(tᵢ)).
PV: Present value of the cash flows ($).
Cᵢ: The i-th cash flow ($).
tᵢ: Time from today until the i-th cash flow (years).
EAR: Effective annual discount rate, as a decimal (per year).
Spreadsheet XNPV works this way, counting days on a 365-day year and discounting to the first date in the list.

scenes.head: Internal rate of return

segs.say: Internal rate of return: 0 = Σₜ₌₀ⁿ Cₜ/(1 + IRR)ᵗ.
IRR: Internal rate of return: the rate per period at which the NPV is zero (per period).
Cₜ: Cash flow at period t, including the time-0 cost ($).
t: Period in which the cash flow arrives (periods).
n: Last period with a cash flow (periods).
It assumes this: Found by trial, interpolation or a spreadsheet; a unique IRR is guaranteed only when the cash flows change sign once.
For a loan or bond bought at a given price and held to maturity, the IRR is its yield to maturity.

scenes.head: Linear interpolation between two trial rates

segs.say: Linear interpolation between two trial rates: IRR ≈ r_L + (r_H − r_L) (NPV_L)/(NPV_L − NPV_H).
r_L: Lower trial rate, where the NPV is positive (per period).
r_H: Higher trial rate, where the NPV is negative (per period).
NPV_L: NPV at the lower rate ($).
NPV_H: NPV at the higher rate ($).
It assumes this: The two trial rates bracket the IRR.
Slightly overstates the IRR of a conventional project; the closer the two trial rates, the smaller the error.

scenes.head: Valuing an uneven contract

segs.say: A fictional events venue signs a three-year agreement with a corporate client, which will pay $2,000 at the end of year 1, $3,000 at the end of year 2 and $5,000 at the end of year 3. The venue discounts at 7% a year. What is the agreement worth today, and what would it be worth at the end of year 3 if every payment were invested at 7%?

scenes.head: Valuing an uneven contract

segs.say: Step 1. Timeline: $2,000 at t = 1, $3,000 at t = 2, $5,000 at t = 3; annual periods at r = 7%.
Step 3. Add the present values, which are now at the same date: $8,570.96 (adding the unrounded values; the rounded ones add to $8,570.97).

scenes.head: Valuing an uneven contract

segs.say: About $8,570.96 today, or $10,499.80 at the end of year 3.

The client promises $10,000 in total, but the agreement is worth $8,570.96 today, because most of the money comes late. If the client offered a lump sum now instead, the venue should accept anything above about $8,571.

chapters.title: Example: Two ways to be paid

scenes.head: Two ways to be paid

segs.say: Brightwell Energy, a fictional battery-storage installer, will finish a $180,000 installation for a school district in nine months. The district offers two payment plans: (A) $180,000 on completion, in 9 months; (B) $50,000 now, $60,000 in 12 months and $80,000 in 24 months. Brightwell discounts at an effective 10% a year. Which plan is worth more today, and up to what discount rate does that remain true?

scenes.head: Two ways to be paid

segs.say: Step 1. Irregular dates, so measure time in years and use the effective annual rate. Plan A: 180,000 ÷ 1.1^(0.75) = 180,000 ÷ 1.074099 = 167,582.24.
Step 3. Compare at today’s date: B is worth $3,078.92 more. It pays $10,000 more in total, and $50,000 of it arrives at once, which together outweigh the wait for the rest.

Step 4. Find the break-even rate by trial on the difference, B − A. At 14% it is +$1,036.43; at 16%, +$138.93; at 17%, −$281.70. Interpolating between 16% and 17%: 16% + 1% × 138.93 ÷ (138.93 + 281.70) = 16.33%.

scenes.head: Two ways to be paid

segs.say: Plan B is worth $170,661.16 today against $167,582.24 for plan A, $3,078.92 more. B stays ahead for any discount rate up to about 16.3% a year.

B pays more in total but later. Its advantage shrinks as the discount rate rises, and for rates between about 16.3% and any realistic rate plan A’s earlier lump sum would be worth more (the difference changes sign twice, so a second break-even exists, at about 201% a year: an example of the multiple-IRR problem). Brightwell’s answer therefore depends on how much the money is worth to it, and on whether it trusts the district to pay in two years; a doubtful payer would call for a higher rate.

chapters.title: Example: Is the cold-brew system worth buying?

scenes.head: Is the cold-brew system worth buying?

segs.say: Lantern can buy a cold-brew brewing system for $24,000 in March 2027. Ana’s estimates of the extra cash it brings in, after its running costs, are $6,000, $8,500, $9,000 and $9,000 in years 1 to 4, plus about $2,500 from selling it at the end of year 4. She requires 12% a year for a risky project like this. Find the NPV and the IRR, and test how sensitive the decision is.

scenes.head: Is the cold-brew system worth buying?

segs.say: Step 1. Set out the timeline from Lantern’s side: −$24,000 at year 0, then the four net inflows, with the resale value added to year 4 ($9,000 + $2,500 = $11,500).
Step 2. Discount each inflow at 12% (see the table) and add: the inflows are worth $25,847.77 today. Subtract the cost: NPV = 25,847.77 − 24,000 = +$1,847.77.

Step 3. Find the IRR by trial. NPV at 14%: +$687.30. At 15%: +$137.42. At 16%: −$393.43. Interpolating between 15% and 16%: 15% + 1% × 137.42 ÷ (137.42 + 393.43) = 15.26%, which a spreadsheet’s IRR confirms (15.26%).
Step 4. Test the estimates. If every year’s cash were 10% lower ($5,400, $7,650, $8,100 and $8,100, with the resale unchanged), the NPV at 12% would be −$578.13.

scenes.head: Is the cold-brew system worth buying?

segs.say: NPV at 12% = +$1,847.77 and IRR ≈ 15.26%: on Ana’s estimates the brewer is worth buying. But a 10% shortfall in the yearly cash turns the NPV negative (−$578.13).

The brewer clears Ana’s 12% hurdle, but not by much: its value rests on her sales estimates. Before signing, she might test them, for example by asking regular office clients whether they would order cold brew. The NPV answers whether to buy; whether to pay with the bank loan or the supplier’s plan is a separate financing decision, valued in module 3.

scenes.head: What is a fixed-rate note worth?

segs.say: Start with Lantern’s note in March 2027: four quarters left and a market rate of 8%. Lower the market rate to 6%, the note’s own rate, and the value becomes exactly $10,000. Raise it, or add quarters, and watch how much of the value comes from the final payment. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: NPV and IRR of the cold-brew system

segs.say: Ana’s cold-brew decision. Move the discount rate and watch the NPV cross zero at the IRR; scale her cash estimates up or down, or change the resale value, to see how fragile the decision is. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Adding cash flows from different dates

segs.say: Adding cash flows from different dates. The note’s payments add up to $10,600, but that number mixes dollars from four dates and is not its value. Discount each flow to one date first; only then add.

scenes.head: Discounting the time-0 cash flow

segs.say: Discounting the time-0 cash flow. A cost paid today is already at time 0: it is not divided by (1 + r). The same slip happens in spreadsheets when the time-0 cost is put inside Excel’s NPV range, which discounts every flow one period too many and divides the true NPV by 1 + r.

scenes.head: A rate that does not match the spacing

segs.say: A rate that does not match the spacing. Quarterly cash flows need a quarterly rate. Discounting the note’s quarterly payments at 8% per quarter gives $7,847.12, far too low. Convert the rate to the period of the cash flows first.

scenes.head: Using the loan rate as the discount rate for a risky project

segs.say: Using the loan rate as the discount rate for a risky project. Discounted at 7.2% a year, roughly the rate on Lantern’s bank loan, the brewer’s NPV would be about $5,007, far more than at the 12% its risk calls for. The rate should reflect the risk of the project’s cash flows, not the cost of the loan that pays for it.

scenes.head: Choosing by IRR between options that exclude each other

segs.say: Choosing by IRR between options that exclude each other. A small project with a high IRR can add less value than a large one with a lower IRR. When only one option can be chosen, pick the higher NPV. And when cash flows change sign more than once, the IRR may not be unique: use the NPV.

scenes.head: Treating an NPV estimate as a fact

segs.say: Treating an NPV estimate as a fact. An NPV is only as good as its cash-flow estimates and rate. The brewer’s +$1,847.77 becomes −$578.13 if each year’s cash is 10% lower. Always recompute the NPV under less favourable assumptions before deciding.

scenes.head: Discounting uneven cash flows is the everyday tool of anyone who prices debt or decides on investments.

segs.say: Discounting uneven cash flows is the everyday tool of anyone who prices debt or decides on investments.

scenes.head: Selling a loan.

segs.say: Selling a loan. Banks sometimes sell loans they have made to other lenders or investors. The buyer prices the remaining payments exactly as this lesson priced Lantern’s note: each payment discounted at the rate the buyer could earn on similar loans today. When market rates have risen since the loans were made, the price is below the amount still owed, and the selling bank records the difference as a loss. The same arithmetic, in reverse, gives a gain when rates have fallen. Nobody has defaulted; only the rate used to discount fixed payments has changed.

scenes.head: Choosing between investments.

segs.say: Choosing between investments. The finance team of a fictional regional airline must decide whether to refurbish the cabins of four aircraft. The spending comes in two bursts, the extra revenue builds up over several years, and the cabins must be refitted again before the aircraft are retired. The team sets out every incremental cash flow on a timeline, discounts at the airline’s required return for projects of this risk, and reports the NPV, the IRR and how both change if passenger demand is weaker than expected. Because the cash flows change sign more than once, the board is told to rely on the NPV.

scenes.head: Comparing payment plans.

segs.say: Comparing payment plans. A fictional university buying a new library system is offered a price of $1.2 million paid on delivery, or a series of uneven payments over three years tied to milestones. The procurement office discounts the milestone payments at the university’s borrowing rate, because a promise to pay is close to a loan, and chooses the plan with the lower present cost. Here the cash flows are outflows, so the better option is the one with the smaller present value.

scenes.head: Ana decides on the cold-brew system the way the airline does.

segs.say: Ana decides on the cold-brew system the way the airline does. On her estimates its NPV at 12% is about +$1,848 and its IRR about 15.3%, so it is worth buying, but a 10% shortfall in sales would turn the NPV negative. She leans towards buying, provided two office clients confirm they will take cold brew regularly. She also keeps the two questions apart: whether the brewer adds value (this lesson) and how to pay for it, with Coastline’s 7.2% loan or the supplier’s “0%” instalment plan, which module 3 answers by valuing each financing option’s payments. And she keeps the Coastline note: at today’s 8%, its 6% rate is worth about $190 to Lantern.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: An uneven cash-flow stream is valued by discounting each cash flow to one date with its own discount factor and adding the results: PV = Σ C_t ÷ (1 + r)ᵗ.
A stream can be valued at any date; values at different dates differ by the factor (1 + r)ᵀ, which gives a check.
The rate per period must match the spacing of the cash flows; for irregular dates, use t in years and the effective annual rate.

Lantern’s Coastline note, four payments of $150 and the $10,000 principal, is worth $9,809.61 in March 2027 at 8% compounded quarterly: less than its face value because its 6% rate is below the market’s. Fixed payments lose value when rates rise.
NPV = Σ C_t ÷ (1 + r)ᵗ from t = 0, with costs negative and only incremental cash flows. Accept a positive NPV; between exclusive options, choose the highest NPV, provided it is positive.

The IRR is the rate at which the NPV is zero, found by trial and interpolation or a spreadsheet. For a conventional project it agrees with the NPV rule; with several sign changes or exclusive options, rely on NPV.
In Excel, NPV() treats its first value as one period away: add the time-0 cash flow outside the function. IRR() takes the whole stream.

scenes.head: Work the guided problems, then take the knowledge check.

segs.say: That is the whole lesson. Now work the guided problems, with hints when you need them, then try the questions on your own and take the knowledge check. A score of 80 percent completes the lesson.
